prime.problem: PyTorch broadcasts silently: a (32, 1) column used against a (32, 27) grid is copied 27 times without any line of code saying so. If you backprop through that line as if nothing was copied, your gradient has the wrong shape or the wrong size, and nothing warns you.
prime.fits: You just walked dlogprobs back to dnorm_logits atom by atom, and micrograd taught you that a value used twice gets its gradients added with +=. This card turns that rule into the tensor version: a broadcast is a value used many times at once.
prime.goal: Look at any forward line where shapes change and write its backward line by flipping sum ↔ broadcast, then finish dlogit_maxes and the second dlogits branch so cmp prints exact.

attend: In (a + b).sum() with b of shape (2, 1), how many separate paths lead from one entry of b to the loss, and what does that do to b.grad?
Which axis do you sum over in the backward pass: the one that was stretched, or the one that was already full size?
Why does subtracting each row's maximum leave the loss unchanged, and what must that mean for dlogit_maxes?
What local derivative does max have for the entries that didn't win, and how does F.one_hot encode it?
What goes wrong in the next broadcast if you drop keepdim=True from the backward sum?

must: Broadcast copies one entry into k places → each copy is a separate use with its own gradient → the chain rule adds uses (micrograd's +=) → backward is a sum over the stretched axis, keeping it as size 1

A sum gives every input a coefficient of 1 in the output → each input's local derivative is 1 → each gets the output's gradient unchanged → backward is a copy (broadcast) of the output gradient back to the input's shape

Softmax is unchanged by shifting a whole row by c → the loss doesn't depend on logit_maxes → its true gradient is 0 → the measured dlogit_maxes (up to 1.02e-8) is float rounding, so skipping its branch still passes allclose

max passes one entry per row through and ignores the rest → local derivative is 1 at the winner, 0 elsewhere → one_hot(indices) * dlogit_maxes routes the gradient only to the winner → the same pattern explains max-pooling's backward
elevated: keepdim=True on the backward sum → result is (32, 1), not (32,) → it broadcasts along the right axis next time; a (32,) tensor aligns with the last axis and fails (27 vs 32) or, worse, silently mis-broadcasts when the sizes happen to match

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the two small graphs (one value copied into three places; three values summed into one) and write the gradient on every edge. Then in 3–4 sentences explain why dlogit_maxes is a sum and why it comes out ≈ 0.
checklist: broadcast = one value used several times → backward adds the gradients from each use
sum = each input enters with coefficient 1 → backward copies the output gradient to each input
sum over the stretched axis with keepdim=True so d<name> has <name>'s shape
shifting a row doesn't change softmax, so the true dlogit_maxes is 0; what you measure is rounding
the max branch goes back through one_hot: only the winning position gets gradient

retrieve.q: Explain, using the chain rule, why a forward broadcast turns into a backward sum rather than a backward copy.
answer: a broadcast is one value used in several places
contributions from several uses of the same value add
so the gradient is the sum of the gradients at all copies

retrieve.q: Walk through norm_logits = logits - logit_maxes backward: what gradient flows into logits, what flows into logit_maxes, and what shape is each?
answer: into logit_maxes: −dnorm_logits, summed over axis 1 with keepdim, shape (32, 1)
logits then gets a second contribution through max: one_hot(indices) * dlogit_maxes, added with +=

retrieve.q: The max branch changes dlogits by at most about 1e-8. Argue for and against writing it in exercise 1, and say what the fused cross-entropy does instead.
answer: for: it makes cmp bit-exact and practises the one-hot routing that max-pooling needs
against: it doesn't change training; the true gradient is exactly 0
fused cross-entropy computes dlogits as softmax − one-hot directly and never mentions logit_maxes

retrieve.q: A forward line is y = x * w with x (32, 64) and w (1, 64). Which of dx, dw needs a sum, over which axis, and why?
answer: w was stretched along axis 0 (32 rows), so dw = (x * dy).sum(0, keepdim=True), shape (1, 64)
x was not stretched, so dx = w * dy with no sum, shape (32, 64)

compare.q: The bias gradient db2 = dlogits.sum(0) on the matmul card and dlogit_maxes here are both sums. What is the common cause, and why is one summed over axis 0 and the other over axis 1?
answer: both variables were broadcast in the forward pass
b2 (27,) was stretched across the 32 rows → sum over axis 0
logit_maxes (32, 1) was stretched across the 27 columns → sum over axis 1
the rule is the same; which axis follows from which dimension was size 1

compare.q: micrograd's += fix for a Value used twice and this card's backward sum: is the sum just the tensor version of +=? How does each one fail if you forget it?
answer: yes: a broadcast is one value used k times at once, and the sum adds the k contributions
forget += in micrograd → the later use overwrites the earlier one; gradient too small
forget the sum here → the gradient has the wrong shape (e.g. (32, 27) for a (32, 1) variable) or you pick one copy and lose the rest

predict.q: Suppose the forward pass subtracted each row's mean instead of its max: m = logits.mean(1, keepdim=True). Would dm still be ≈ 0? What would the second branch into dlogits look like, and how is it different from the one-hot branch?
predict.answer: Still ≈ 0: any per-row shift cancels in the softmax, so the loss doesn't depend on m. But the mean uses every entry with coefficient 1/27, so its backward is a copy of dm/27 to all 27 positions, a dense broadcast, instead of the one-hot's single winner. Both contributions are float noise here.

apply.task: In labs/sum-broadcast-duality.py, change the toy's forward sum x.sum(1, keepdim=True) to x.mean(1, keepdim=True), keeping the weights 10 and 20. Predict x.grad on paper first, then run it.
apply.done: Your prediction matches the run: x.grad is 3.3333 in every entry of row 0 and 6.6667 in every entry of row 1 (10/3 and 20/3).
apply.hint: A mean is a sum times 1/3, so its backward is a copy of the upstream gradient times 1/3.
